articles.title: Elbows up, phones down: Some Canadians who travel to the US are keeping it off social media
articles.summary: Some Canadians who’ve crossed the border into the United States feel uneasy about how their trips will be perceived. So they’re keeping their travels under wraps.
articles.body: Stefanie Ricchio has been taking her kids to New York City since they were newborns. “It’s a special place for us and a tradition for my daughter,” says the Toronto-based chartered professional accountant. To celebrate her daughter’s birthday each April, they travel to the city to watch a Yankees game at Yankee Stadium. But this year, while they still made the trip, they kept quiet about it. “I felt like this is not really something that I want to broadcast because I feel like I shouldn’t be spending my money there,” she says. “There’s that conflict of (being a) super-proud Canadian, but also these are our traditions and memories that mean something to my daughter that I didn’t want to give up.” Ricchio is referring to the reluctance — by now, a grassroots national resistance — of Canadians traveling to the United States. Alongside the buy-Canadian movement, which started when US President Donald Trump first started imposing tariffs in March 2025 and continues to today, Canadians also changed their travel plans. In 2024, Canadians made 39 million return trips across the US-Canada border. Then the tariffs and 51st state mentions began and that number contracted — sharply. There were year-over-year declines in Canadians traveling to the US for 15 consecutive months until April 2026. The 2026 Canadian Travel and Tourism Outlook study from Environics Research shows that six in 10 Canadians are either actively avoiding travel to the US (46%) or would travel to the US, but feel conflicted (15%). This summer, however, there was a slow but steady increase of Canadians crossing the border, according to Statistics Canada, though numbers were still 25.6% lower than in the same time period in 2024. Like Ricchio, they are traveling to sports games, concerts and theme parks. Many of them, however, aren’t posting their trips on social media or talking about the holidays with friends because the “elbows up” sentiment still prevails. “If I did have to tell somebody that I was going, I felt a little bit of angst. Are they judging me? Saying, ‘You could just watch the Yankees play here in Toronto,’” she says. ‘The reality is, I’m not going to the US to visit Donald Trump’ Kemi Wells-Conrad, founder and president of Wells Luxury Travel, a travel agency in Vancouver, says her travelers are falling into two categories. Recent tensions between the two countries have led some of her clients to restrict US travel entirely, canceling US trips they may have planned and even avoiding layovers at US airports. Others, particularly those traveling with family, are “still going,” she says. “Because Hawaii, for example, is so good with family resorts and it might be their annual tradition, or some of them have a home in Arizona or one of the Hawaiian islands. “I definitely had people saying, ‘Oh, I’m not telling my friends I’m going,’ or ‘not posting on social media that I’m going,’” Wells-Conrad says. But she explains that they tend to separate Hawaii, in particular, from the rest of the US. “Even though, of course, it’s part of the United States, people do see it differently with the different culture.” Barry Choi, a personal finance and loyalty program expert in Toronto, travels to the US for both work and fun. When the tensions between Canada and the US first started, he kept quiet about the trips, but now he shares both on his Instagram account to more than 12,000 followers — something he’s gotten backlash for. “The reality is, I’m not going to the US to visit Donald Trump. I go there to see friends, family, and things that we don’t have here in Canada. If there was like a Disney World in Vaughan,” he says, referring to a suburb of Toronto, “of course I wouldn’t go to Orlando. Or if my friends and family lived here in Canada rather than Miami, California, New York, there’d be no reason to go.” He decided to start posting these travels publicly because he thought it worthwhile to share with those who follow his social media accounts what the experience is like for Canadians. “I was in the Palm Beaches, and every single local I talked to, as soon as I told them I’m from Canada, apologized for the president,” Choi says. “They’re like, “I didn’t vote for him. Most people here do not like him. I found that to be a bit shocking, to be honest.” The tariffs and tensions are affecting people on both sides of the border, he says. “I do feel like the people there are feeling the same struggles as us.” ‘The vibe has completely shifted’ Still, some who have ventured across the border have decided it’s not worth it. Caleigh, a marketing executive in Toronto who didn’t want her last name published for fear of backlash, recently drove across the border to watch a Hayley Williams concert in upstate New York, but kept quiet about the trip. “I know that my family is very much like against it, and friends are apprehensive,” she says of US travel. She had considered not going at all and listing the tickets for resale. “All of the Lake Ontario rhetoric was a week or so before the concert, and then more tariffs were put into place, so there was a heightened sense of everything going on,” she says. The plan was to drive across with a friend, but they wondered, “Is the border going to be stricter now?” In the end, she and a friend drove to the show. Normally, she would have posted her road trip and the concert to her social media, but she didn’t post at all during the journey. Part of it was not wanting people who follow her to know she had gone, the other reason was concern over having her phone searched at the border. While her phone wasn’t searched going into the US, her car was. “As a family, we used to go to upstate New York quite a lot growing up, and (this time) felt completely different. They were doing flashlight searches of all the cars, no matter what,” she says. “The vibe has completely shifted. The kind of scrutiny has completely shifted.” As a result, she doesn’t plan on making another trip — whether she keeps quiet about it or not.

articles.title: Bessbrook: Pair sentenced for human trafficking crimes
articles.summary: The pair were arrested in November 2022 in what was described at the time as the PSNI's largest operation against human trafficking.
articles.body:
A man and woman have been sentenced for a series of offences including human trafficking.

Gerald Corrigan, 66, of Keeragh Park, Pomeroy, previously pleaded guilty to human trafficking, possessing criminal property and transferring criminal property. He was sentenced to 16 months; this was broken down as eight months in custody and eight months on license.

Mavie Martins Mariano 51, of Ard Aveen Park, Bessbrook, previously pleaded guilty to human trafficking, acquiring criminal property, possessing criminal property, transferring criminal property, brothel keeping and controlling prostitution.

Mariano, who is originally from Brazil, was given a three year sentence.

This is broken down as three months in custody and 33 months on license.

The court heard that both defendants had already spent time in custody on remand and therefore it was likely that time in custody had been served.

Speaking at Dungannon Crown Court on Tuesday, Judge Brian Sherrard said he took into account the fact that both defendants had pleaded guilty and had expressed remorse.

He said he also considered the impact of imprisonment on Mariano's family and Corrigan's health issues when delivering his sentence.

Judge Sherrard said: "You were both concerned in the trafficking of women for the purpose of sexual exploitation and you both acquired a considerable amount of money during this offending period."

He added: "I acknowledge this is not a case involving threats or violence and it is accepted by the prosecution in this case there is no evidence of coercion and the defence contend these women were acting voluntarily."

The pair were arrested in November 2022 in what was described at the time as the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) largest operation against human trafficking.

During the operation police said that 27 brothels were raided across Northern Ireland, with some 150 officers involved.

The offences took place between 23 March 2020 and 21 November 2022.

The court had previously heard that a large amount of money in the region of £174,000 was transferred between the two defendants.

At a previous sentencing hearing in Dungannon Crown Court on 22 September the prosecution summarised their case against Corrigan and Mariano.

The prosecution said the case boiled down to "the organisation of sex work and controlling of prostitution" in an operation that spread throughout Northern Ireland over a period of two years and eight months.

In relation to Mariano, a prosecuting barrister said she had a lead role in the offending and there was evidence that £174,000 passed between the accounts of the two defendants.

The barrister said that Mariano had admitted at police interview to being involved in the booking of property for women described as "escorts" and that an apartment had been booked by her on 22 occasions for "sex workers".

The prosecuting barrister added that "once you get into arranging the properties and organising them, it is controlling prostitution".

The prosecution said Mariano had also admitted during police interview to helping to organise escort adverts and organising the moving of around "five to six girls a week".

The judge asked if there had been any "evidence of lifestyle change or any large amounts of money benefiting her".

The prosecuting barrister outlined that Mariano had funded a trip to Turkey for gastric implant surgery for a "not insignificant amount".

A prosecution barrister also said that the case revolved around "the exploitation of sex workers" and there was "always harm in this type of offending" adding that "it is built into it".

In relation to Corrigan, the prosecution outlined how he was primarily a driver of sex workers and he had a role of getting and collecting money.

A prosecution barrister said that Corrigan had accepted he had "lodged money into his bank account knowing the money came from prostitution".

A prosecution barrister also said Corrigan's role was "the moving of sex workers with the knowledge and acceptance that were being exploited".

One of the central arguments from the defence barristers in the case was there was no sign of coercion of the women in these cases.

A defence barrister also addressed the prosecution's point about Mariano's trip to Turkey.

A defence barrister said: "In respect of when the prosecution can only muster that this lady went to Turkey to get a gastric band fitted, this speaks for itself.

"Citizens have been advised not to go Turkey because [these procedures are] alarmingly cheap and inquests have identified that people have died.

"This lady does not have money, she has no trappings of wealth, zero, had she had money she would have went privately to somewhere like Dublin."

On Mariano's role a defence barrister added that she was "not a principal, she was not an organiser and she played no leading role".

The defence barrister also raised concerns about the impact that a custodial sentence for Mariano could have on her family.

A defence barrister added: "There was no coercion in this case, these were adult women engaging in sex work voluntarily".

Commenting on Corrigan's role, a defence barrister said that he "wasn't involved in the overall scheme, he knew he was driving prostitutes, but any planning was limited" and that he gained "a very modest amount of financial gain".

A defence barrister also outlined that Corrigan had already spent 10 months in jail and that he suffered from ill health, including prostate cancer.

Det Insp Rachel Miskelly, from the Police Service of Northern Ireland's organised crime branch, said many of the victims were originally from Brazil and were brought here with "false promises of a better life".

"We believe the victims were specifically targeted due to their vulnerability, namely their lack of English language and their immigration status," she said.

"This is so typical of what human traffickers do. They prey on victims who are in any way vulnerable, and those who are afraid or unable to speak out."

articles.title: ‘Doing a real disservice’: Annamalai backs CJP leaders, questions their continued custody
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu BJP president K Annamalai on Tuesday expressed Cockroach Janata Party and questioned Delhi Police's handling of the case
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu BJP president K Annamalai on Tuesday expressed Cockroach Janata Party and questioned Delhi Police's handling of the case against its leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.While talking to reporters, Annamalai said that continued judicial custody of CJP leaders raises concerns about the rule of law."I'm a little bit concerned in our country. I have a feeling they (Delhi Police) have taken the law into their hands, and the judge gets recused... I may not agree with many of the CJP's modes of protest. I may not agree with some of the antics of CJP. That's a different argument. But I completely support CJP in terms of the questions they want to raise."It is for the government to answer. But to arrest them for a violation and again to drag them in terms of how they spend their time in jail, that is only going to make the leaders of CJP stronger. I'm afraid of saying that the Delhi police are doing a real disservice," he added.He also said that Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi has every right to question the SIR process, but institutional damage should not be caused."Rahul Gandhi has every right to question the SIR process, but institutional damage should not be caused," he further said.Earlier on Monday, a Delhi court extended the CJP leaders' judicial custody by two days for allegedly entering Jantar Mantar, which is no longer a designated protest venue, and obstructing police personnel on duty.Along with other CJP workers, they waved the national flag at the site and raised slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive custody.According to their lawyer, their bail sureties were rejected due to a reported mismatch in documents. They will now be produced before the court on Wednesday.Meanwhile, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership and praised Das and Ranka for remaining defiant despite spending five days in judicial custody."You must be feeling very strong keeping a 26-year-old Saurav Das in jail. You must be feeling very strong beating children on the streets. You must be feeling very strong putting up barricades across Delhi and dragging students on the streets," he said.Dipke claimed that Das and Ranka had gone to Jantar Mantar to wave the national flag but were sent to judicial custody. He also alleged that their court hearings had been repeatedly postponed. "Is this strength? Hiding behind the police, hiding behind the courts, is this Narendra Modi's strength?" he asked.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
articles.summary: Leaders of the movement for independence vow to push on but the margin of defeat could make that difficult.
articles.body:
It was a decisive result in a referendum that could have strained the bonds of national unity.

But preliminary results show that more than two-thirds of Alberta voters sent a clear message that they want to remain in Canada.

It's possible that once the final tally is counted, the rejection by a comfortable majority of voters to pursue separation through a binding referendum could halt Alberta's separatist sentiment in its tracks.

This would push the idea that had been discussed quietly for decades back into the political fringes.

For leaders of the Alberta separatist movement, while the result was expected given the polling, it was still disappointing after more than a year of campaigning and pushing for a vote on separation.

Asked by the BBC how he felt in one sentence after the results, separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre simply said: "Not happy".

The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice".

But the movement's leaders say their battle is long from over and that the issue could dominate Alberta politics for years to come.

Jeffrey Rath, a Calgary-lawyer and one of the main spokespeople for Alberta separation, said he and others "plan to roll up our sleeves and work harder".

Keith Wilson, another separatist, told supporters in Calgary that while the vote is over, "the conversation about Alberta's future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue".

Smith, who openly supported and campaigned for the unity vote, thanked voters for the result.

The Alberta premier has been criticised for taking a "dangerous" gamble that the independence push would likely face defeat while still giving her restive base what they wanted.

She lowered the petition threshold needed to get the citizen-led campaign the ballot in the first place.

How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada

Carney pitches oil pipeline as a response to US-Canada trade war

At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation

By making Monday's result non-binding, she got around a court decision blocking the pro-separation petition because it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated.

That gamble could test her leadership of the United Conservative Party, which she has led since 2022.

"She's lost the confidence of the (party) base," said Rath.

Albertans who voted against an independence referendum told the BBC throughout the campaign that they were motivated by a desire to keep the country united, especially as Canada grapples with tariff threats from the US, its longtime ally.

They also feared that an independent Alberta could be vulnerable to outside influence - or even annexation.

Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent pro-unity campaigner, told a crowd of supporters on Monday night that the early results made him proud to be Albertan.

At a pro-unity results watch party in Edmonton, Lukaszuk appealled directly to separatists, saying that "some of the issues they have raised are legitimate", and that the province must do the hard work of healing the divisions laid bare by this debate.

"I don't want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again," Lukaszuk said.

Premier Smith told CBC earlier in the week that she would not hold an independence referendum if Albertans vote against it as long as she is premier.

Some of the rifts can't easily be smoothed over.

The separatist sentiment has its roots in "western alienation" which is a term that has been used for decades by some in Canada's western provinces to describe a feeling of being ignored or overlooked by the federal government in central Canada.

Alberta independence supporters - and many on the unity side - believe that Ottawa has long undermined the province's oil and gas industry, most recently through environmental policies.

That anger later deepened as some Albertans grew frustrated with the response by former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the Covid-19 pandemic and vaccine mandates, viewing them as yet another example of government overreach.

Carney, who was raised in Alberta, has worked with Smith to address some of these issues, signing an agreement that would see a new pipeline from Alberta built to Canada's pacific coast.

He nodded to that in his statement on Monday night, saying that his plan is to unlock Canada's "full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core".

But there are signs that there could be tension in the future between Carney and Smith, an able politician and a survivor - so far - of Alberta's rough and tumble politics.

She also put nine other questions to Albertans on Monday, most that seek to give the province more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters like immigration.

The (very) preliminary results suggest that many might pass.

Some who voted in favour of a second binding separation referendum have said they didn't want outright independence, but some leverage over Ottawa. Smith has said these other nine questions help give her just that.

Quebec, another province with similar sovereigntist sentiments, could offer clues on where Alberta's separation movement might end up.

They held two separation referendums, in 1980 and 1995, both of which were defeated by a close margin.

Alberta independence supporters don't hide the fact that they gain inspiration from the majority French-speaking province.

They view Quebec as having successfully used the threat of separation to gain significantly more autonomy over provincial affairs.

And despite support for Quebec sovereignty being at historic lows, a newly elected provincial government has pledged to hold a third referendum on independence by 2030.

Rath made a note of that as he pondered his side's defeat.

The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois "has just formed the government of Quebec with 28% of the vote," he said.

"It's not out of the realm of possibility", he added, that Alberta separatists could do the same in the future.

articles.title: Defund the police betrayed Black America. I'm rebuilding what activists broke
articles.summary: Project H.O.O.D. invited Chicago police officers to meet kids on the South Side, working to undo years of fear fueled by the defund the police movement.
articles.body: In my neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, too many of our residents, especially the children, fear the police. They have been taught that the police are not their friends, that officers might shoot them, arrest them for being Black, and that they are their enemies. I do not believe any of this, and I have sought to correct these misperceptions, which could have fatal consequences. I recently invited several Chicago police officers to visit my community center, Project H.O.O.D. They came in full Chicago blue uniforms, with their police visor caps with the checkered bands, and their guns. At first, there was tension in the room. You could feel it. Some of the kids hid behind the adults, some of whom stood defiantly. The gulf was profound, and that is why I invited the police in to do my part to repair the damage done by the defund the police movement, one encounter at a time. This damage goes back years, a lifetime for most of our youth who know nothing but hostility to the police. For more than a decade, Black Lives Matter and its allies conditioned a generation to treat the police as the problem. Fear and hatred of the police had always been there to some degree in the Black community. CONTROVERSIAL SOCIALIST CHEF FLIP-FLOPS ON ABOLISH THE POLICE, SAYS SHE’S ‘SERIOUS ABOUT PUBLIC SAFETY’ But there was something different about this conditioning, which began to take off after Trayvon Martin’s death in 2012. When George Zimmerman was acquitted, the phrase "Black Lives Matter" was born, and the message that began to spread was that the police were hunting Black boys. Zimmerman was not a police officer, but for the sake of the narrative, he was made the stand-in as the neighborhood vigilante. Michael Brown’s death in Ferguson in 2014 only reinforced the narrative. "Hands up, don’t shoot" became a slogan that was not true. Brown did not have his hands up — instead, he charged the cop, but the image of a White cop and a dead Black teen was all the narrative needed to continue. Police officers nationwide were demonized as an occupying force rather than neighbors with badges. I have watched that fear take root in kids who have already lost too much. It is one of the lasting wounds of the defund era: not only fewer officers on the street, but a generation that learned the people sworn to protect them cannot be trusted. By the time George Floyd died in Minneapolis in 2020, the groundwork had already been laid. The New York Times published its May 30 opinion piece titled "No More Money for the Police," arguing that the path to safety was to reduce police power and contact with the public and redirect the money elsewhere. In Minneapolis, a majority of the City Council stood in a park and pledged to dismantle the police department. The loudest voices were not asking for better training or more accountability. They wanted abolition. When I heard that, I knew one thing: it would be us who paid the price. Not the folks living in leafy suburbs with Black Lives Matter signs in their front yards. And the impact was felt immediately. No police officer wanted to risk going viral. They pulled back. And, shamefully, many in my community demanded that. MR T TAUGHT ME A LESSON EVERY KID ON CHICAGO'S SOUTH SIDE NEEDS TO HEAR In 2019, Chicago recorded roughly 500 homicides. In 2020, that number climbed to 781. In 2021, it reached 804 — the city’s deadliest year in a quarter-century. The spike was national — FBI data showed murders rose nearly 30% in 2020, the largest single-year increase on record, with Black Americans hit even harder. Chicago’s South and West Sides absorbed a disproportionate share. Police staffing fell as retirements and resignations surged. Morale collapsed under canceled days off, forced overtime and the constant message that the job itself was illegitimate. Arrests and proactive policing dropped. The outcome was not a policy experiment. There were more funerals in the neighborhoods that could least afford them. So many of those who died during this time should be alive. They died because Black activists demonized the police to advance their own activist agendas, which led to the very destruction of the people they claimed to be helping. To date, none have taken responsibility for their deadly rhetoric. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION There is nothing I can do about the dead. My focus has been on the living, especially the young minds. They are the ones still paying the price. Years of being told that the police are the enemy taught some of them never to call when something bad is happening. They see the uniform and assume hostility rather than help. I have watched that fear take root in kids who have already lost too much. It is one of the lasting wounds of the defund era: not only fewer officers on the street, but a generation that learned the people sworn to protect them cannot be trusted. At Project H.O.O.D., we are repairing that damage the only way I know how — by bringing the police into our building and letting our kids see them as people. Officers come in and sit with the children, the teenagers and the adults who walk through our doors. They answer questions. They listen to the stories that our young people carry. They show that the uniform does not hide a monster; it covers a man or woman who chose a hard job because they want to keep this community safe. Some of the kids who used to freeze up at the sight of a squad car now stay after and keep talking. A few have even started asking what it takes to become an officer themselves. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The fear does not disappear in a single afternoon, but the wall starts to crack. That is the work. It is not a press conference. It is not a slogan. It is one conversation at a time inside a building where we refuse to let the lies of the last decade become the future of the next one. The police are not the enemy. Treating them as if they are has already cost too many lives on these streets. We are done accepting that. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM PASTOR COREY BROOKS

articles.title: Three months of PM Andy Burnham: Can he sustain the ‘hope vibe’?
articles.summary: The UK’s new prime minister has made big promises and is a popular leader, but there is still talk of an early election.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – There was a moment towards the end of Andy Burnham’s conference speech in Liverpool that, through silence, spoke volumes.

The new prime minister and Labour leader fell quiet.

For 20 seconds he stood, saying nothing. He hadn’t forgotten his words. He was gathering his emotions for a passage of the speech he hadn’t been able to make it through in rehearsals without crying.

Burnham’s father had died just a couple of weeks before, and this was the section where he’d talk about it.

As the audience realised what was coming they stood, applauding, and urging him on with shouts of “Come on, lad!’ and “Come on, Andy!”

Thanking them, he composed himself and continued.

Conference speeches are theatre, and contemporary British political standards require that a leader be relatable. But there’s little doubt that Andy Burnham handled this moment with an emotional register that struck many as genuine.

His predecessor Keir Starmer sometimes came across as wooden, almost robotic and uncomfortable in front of cameras. Burnham, the seventh prime minister in 10 years, is more emotional.

He talks big ideas and grand solutions and relishes the opportunity to communicate.

In the vibes-denominated currency of modern political discourse, this matters.

The polls speak for themselves. Politico’s Poll of Polls had the Labour Party retake top spot shortly after Burnham became PM – a position it has not relinquished since. At the end of September, Ipsos found Andy Burnham to be the only politician with a positive net favourability rating.

YouGov’s polling also judges him the most popular politician in the UK at the moment.

But to keep up, Burnham must deliver tangible change before the next general election. Unless he calls one early, that will be 2029.

According to political analyst Sam Freedman, “So many in Westminster keep coming back to an early election, despite Burnham ruling it out … No one can quite figure out how Burnham keeps the hope vibe going for three more years with relatively little visible progress.”

‘Going back to what Labour was in the 50s’

In the Welsh town of Port Talbot, terraces of workers’ cottages cluster beside the UK’s largest steelworks.

Like much of Wales, Port Talbot did vote Labour for a century – until elections for the Senedd Cymru or Welsh Parliament in May.

Labour was beaten to an unprecedented third place behind Plaid Cymru’s nationalists, and the anti-immigration Reform UK.

Myles Lewis, who organises social walks for the town’s elderly, told Al Jazeera that Labour had not convinced people on immigration, and Starmer’s communication wasn’t good enough.

“[But now], it’s kind of going back to what Labour was in the 50s and 60s, where they actually looked after the working-class people. I do believe Andy Burnham can get there because I think he has the interests of the working-class people.”

In his first weeks in power, Burnham delivered a quick flurry of eye-catching, domestic, cost-of-living-focused policies.

He capped bus fares, cut the value-added tax (VAT) on electricity bills, and cut business rates for pubs.

He said that he would end street homelessness, reindustrialise the country, take services back into public control, and start the biggest build-out of social housing since World War II.

The mayor of Greater Manchester for nine years, Burnham supports the devolution of powers from Westminster to the UK’s nations and regions.

In July, he announced mayors could keep a share of business rates from April 2027 and of income tax from 2028.

And his conference speech in September set out the contours of some big political battles to come, including a national social care service, free at the point of use, paid for by changing the UK pensions’ triple lock from 2030. It would arrive next parliament. Burnham also pitched a national commission on electoral reform, with a manifesto commitment to overhaul the voting system. And he delivered a blunt verdict on Brexit: that it “has done more harm than good”. He wouldn’t rule out an in-out referendum, or a pledge for the UK to rejoin the European Union, in Labour’s next manifesto, he said.

On foreign affairs, there is less blue water between Burnham and his predecessors.

When he travelled to Ukraine in August, the UK’s new prime minister came with a headline-grabbing gift – British know-how to build the long-range SCALP missile. He was the fourth British prime minister to visit Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and pledge steadfast support.

On Gaza, he has said the Labour government “didn’t get it right” and should have called for a ceasefire earlier. And in September, the Burnham government announced a sanctions package against illegal West Bank settlements.

But there has been no genocide declaration, and no full arms embargo against Israel. And Burnham hasn’t overturned the Starmer government’s proscription of the Palestine Action protest group as a “terrorist” organisation.

Defence spending is also a looming problem.

The government’s formal defence pledge is 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035, and Burnham has declined to say whether he’d pay for it with tax rises or welfare cuts.

John Healey, who resigned as the UK’s defence secretary in June over underfunding, is now chancellor of the exchequer, and will not commit to the 3-percent-by-2030 target he set himself.

Burnham’s first budget comes at the end of this month. A full spending review follows next year. Much will be clearer after these.

His biggest pledges – reindustrialisation, control of public services, a new social care system – are expensive.

Burnham certainly has the vibes. The public likes them, for now. The budget will show whether he can afford them.

articles.title: Memo from New Delhi: Make America India Again?
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: First, he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. Then he wanted Lake Ontario to be called Lake America.
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: First, he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. Then he wanted Lake Ontario to be called Lake America. Now he wants New Mexico to become New America. At this rate, goes the joke, US President Donald Trump may soon rename America itself – perhaps call it New India, since Christopher Columbus, whose voyages helped bring the continent to European attention, was looking for India when he got here.“New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!” Trump declared on Truth Social on Monday. The new name, he promised, would add “great value and prestige” to the state, boost residents’ pride in saluting the American flag and even ensure that “the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!”New Mexico’s political reps were unimpressed. Senator Ben Ray Lujan, a Democrat, reminded Trump that the state’s name dates back centuries, long before the United States itself came into existence. “We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico,” he shot back.There is also a constitutional obstacle to the Trump threat, which some see as trolling: the state’s constitution does the naming and a presidential social media post cannot change that. Renaming it would require action through the state’s constitutional and legislative processes, as well as Congress. “No, Mr. Trump. The American people don’t want you to rename New Mexico... They want you to immediately end your illegal Iran War that is forcing Americans to pay $4.30 a gallon for gas and $6.30 a gallon for diesel. Enough,” clapped back Senator Bernie Sanders.New Mexico’s history stretches much further back than that of the country Trump wants to insert into its name. Spanish explorers entered the region in the 16th century, and Santa Fe, New Mexico’s capital, was established in 1610, decades before the English settlement at Plymouth and more than 150 years before American independence in 1776. Indigenous peoples had inhabited the region long before the Spanish arrived.The question of who named America is itself a reminder that geography and nomenclature have rarely followed a straightforward path. The name America was popularised by German cartographer Martin Waldseemuller, who used it on a world map in 1507 in honour of Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci, whose accounts helped persuade Europeans that the lands across the Atlantic were a separate continent, rather than part of Asia.Christopher Columbus, meanwhile, had sailed west seeking a route to India, and he died in 1506 still believing he had reached India. Spain consequently referred to its American possessions as the West Indies, distinguishing them from the East Indies he had hoped to reach. Early European maps also used terms such as the New World and, in some cases, India Nova, or New India.In short, America was named after Vespucci, not Columbus, although Columbus’s voyages helped set the European encounter in motion. A Genoese navigator sailing for Spain went looking for India; a German mapmaker honoured an Italian explorer; and an entire continent acquired a name born of that chain of events. Truly, the 16th-century branding industry was nothing if not international.Indeed, cartographers note the continent was hardly nameless before Europeans arrived with their maps. Various indigenous tribes, notably the Lenape, Iroquois, and Anishinaabe, called America Turtle Island, referring to the creation story where the continent was built on the back of a giant turtle. Abya Yala, a term used by the Guna people of Panama, has gained wider currency among Indigenous activists as a name for the Americas. Many American states have indigenous names: Alabama, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Wisconsin and Wyoming among them.So if historical authenticity is the new test, trolls are suggesting that Trump could widen his campaign to rename Virginia (named after England’s Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen); Maryland – honouring Queen Henrietta Maria; and New York, which commemorates a British duke. Restoring Indigenous place names where historically justified might be a more meaningful exercise than replacing an old name with what sounds like a real-estate development.There is also irony in the term “American-Indian” itself. Columbus’s geographical mistake helped give rise to the label applied to Indigenous Americans – Indians, and pejoratively, “Red Indians.” Clearly, Europeans’ confusion about where they had arrived left a lasting – and deadly – imprint on the people they encountered. So if Trump really wants to correct history’s naming errors, perhaps, chuckled one wag, he could start at home and rename America as New India, in honour of Columbus’s original destination.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
articles.summary: The bank says workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week from February.
articles.body:
The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home.

NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February.

The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility.

But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs.

Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic.

In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home.

Other firms such as Boots and JP Morgan have brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day.

But Barclays faced a backlash from staff last month over plans to require workers to go to the office three days a week. It brought in a longer transition period in response to staff and union complaints.

Unite said NatWest was abolishing its "remote first" employment category, which allows 13,497 workers to attend the office around twice a month, and requiring 17,272 hybrid workers to increase their office attendance.

The union says that many of the affected workers are lower-paid grades, and the new requirements will increase cost-of-living pressures, while disrupting the arrangements of disabled workers and carers.

In a statement, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham called NatWest's move a "kick in the teeth" for its workers.

"Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities," she said

"For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce."

Graham called on NatWest to "ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers".

A NatWest spokesman said: "Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we've also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers - helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.

"That's why we're introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area.

"We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we're giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition."

articles.title: Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises
articles.summary: Government forces launch major offensives across multiple Yemeni front lines as a tightening blockade threatens Taiz.
articles.body:
The siege on Taiz has cut humanitarian supplies to the Yemeni city, the United Nations has warned, and left many of its inhabitants without food and other essentials.

UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said on Tuesday that the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), who have surrounded the city, must immediately allow humanitarian relief to enter or risk a catastrophe.

“The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” the high commissioner said.

“Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated. Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely.”

Taiz, which has been repeatedly besieged throughout the war, has been encircled again by the Houthis after they captured a major road linking the city to southern Yemen.

The humanitarian situation in Taiz is reaching a breaking point with the prices of basic commodities multiplying in price, amid shortages of some goods.

Continued fighting in Taiz governorate has also killed at least 32 civilians between August 1 and October 19, including 14 children. There are fears of more deaths as fighting approaches the city.

“I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects,” Turk said.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government had appealed to the United Nations to intervene and lift the blockade, warning that the Houthi siege threatens more than 4 million people.

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that shifting front lines and road closures have cut off 800,000 people from life-saving assistance, the vast majority located in Taiz. Nationwide, more than 18 million Yemenis face severe food insecurity.

Forces aligned with the internationally-recognised government on Monday launched air strikes in Taiz governorate that destroyed Houthi reinforcements in Najd Qasim and a weapons depot in Jabal Habashi.

The Yemeni government added on Tuesday that its forces had stopped Houthi attempts to advance across Taiz, incuding in al-Shaqab, al-Misrakh, al-Aqroudh, and Jabal Han.

On Tuesday, local authorities raised the death toll from a Houthi attack on a military base in Shabwa governorate to 73.

Monday’s Houthi ballistic missile strikes on al-Alam camp were condemned by the Yemeni government as a “treacherous bloody assault” and a war crime.

President of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi formally requested the UN to designate the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation”.

The United Kingdom said on Tuesday it would deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, after cities and infrastructure were targeted in rocket and drone attacks.

The British Ministry of Defence said that Typhoon warplanes would play a “defensive role” only and would not carry out attacks in Yemen.

Egypt’s parliament meanwhile delayed a vote on Monday to authorise the military to support Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Ali al-Dahab, a military and security strategic affairs expert, said that while there appears to be more international support for the anti-Houthi alliance, this will not likely translate into boots on the ground in Yemen.

“The probability of international ground forces engaging to confront the Houthis seems slim; expected participation will be limited to air and naval support,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Yemeni military launched a sweeping offensive dubbed “Dawn of Yemen” on 5 October to reverse recent Houthi advances. But despite initial successes in the early days of the campaign, with hundreds of Houthi fighters reportedly killed in air strikes, there are questions about whether these counter-offensives have run out of steam.

“The transition from defence to offence remains limited on the ground, and the map of the Yemeni government’s influence in al-Marib [an energy-rich part of central Yemen] has not expanded to the extent implied by the meaning of the [operation],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.

“Government forces must exploit the gaps created by conventional and drone air strikes in Houthi ranks by launching a multi-directional operation that turns this into a strategic shift, specifically in the northwestern direction toward Sanaa.”

The intensification of ground battles in Yemen has triggered a wave of cross-border attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The attack prompted the Saudi Civil Defense to activate early warning platforms across the capital.

The Arab coalition has launched waves of strikes on Houthi positions across Yemen during the past week.

“On the strategic and long-term, [aerial attrition strikes] can have a tangible impact on the Houthis’ military infrastructure, structures, machines, and vehicles,” al-Dahab said.

However, he questioned the government’s ability to capitalise on these strikes on the western coast, where the Yemeni government is attempting to claw back losses from the Houthis.

“Do government forces have enough power to launch an attack toward Mocha on the coast or toward Hodeidah?” al-Dahab asked, noting that Houthi fighters are desperately holding onto the Kahboub mountains in Lahij for their commanding maritime view over the Gulf of Aden and the southern Red Sea.

articles.title: Identify, defeat forces against India: Modi calls for unity, self-reliance
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Calling for a united fight against forces seeking to divide society, undermine India's dignity and attack its culture, Prime Minister Narendra
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Calling for a united fight against forces seeking to divide society, undermine India's dignity and attack its culture, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday urged all political parties and national institutions to put the country first. Stressing that national self-respect and faith in one's own strength were essential for progress, he said India must protect its cultural identity while building the capabilities to overcome challenges without depending on others.“We must identify the enemies of Mother India. We must defeat them,” Modi said at the Vijayadashami celebrations in east Delhi. “The forces that hurt the honour and dignity of the country, the people who divide society, the mentality of those who hate our culture — these are the enemies of the country.”Quoting a Vedic verse, Modi said all institutions and political parties must stand together in the national interest. “We must fight the enemies of the country together,” he said, calling for a collective commitment to “Nation First”.His remarks came hours after RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, speaking in Nagpur, cited political upheavals in France, Albania, Nepal and Bangladesh while warning against attempts to bring about regime change in India. Bhagwat also cautioned against protests becoming political tools and urged both authorities and protesters to remain within constitutional limits.Linking national progress to cultural identity, Modi said, “A nation progresses only when it has a sense of self-respect,” adding that heritage played an important role in building that confidence.He said India's cultural treasures had been looted and taken abroad for centuries, but efforts were now underway to restore them. Over 650 ancient idols had been brought back in the past 12 years, he said, also highlighting UNESCO recognition for Indian heritage sites and Diwali.Drawing lessons from Lord Ram's life, Modi stressed self-reliance. Despite the ocean separating him from Lanka, Ram mobilised collective strength, brought together available resources and achieved what appeared impossible.“We must not sit relying on others. We must recognise our own strength. We must have faith in our own resources,” he said, linking the message to the goals of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat.Describing Vijayadashami as the victory of truth over falsehood, Modi also recalled Ram embracing Nishad Raj and honouring Shabari as examples of compassion and inclusion.He said Ram Rajya represented governance without discrimination, where everyone received justice and equal opportunities. “The objective of power is not to rule, but public welfare,” he said, urging service to the poor and deprived.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
articles.summary: The sixth report from Covid inquiry criticises the lack of PPE and the way patients were discharged from hospital.
articles.body:
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.

The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.

There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.

It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.

Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.

Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.

Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".

"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.

"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."

Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

Lack of PPE and financial support for carers

At the start of the pandemic, the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock said the government had placed a protective ring around care homes.

But the report said that this claim was unfounded.

a lack of PPE meant staff had to resort to make-shift workarounds, including bins bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls

the decision to discharge hospitals patients into care homes at the start of the pandemic was understandable, but guidance should have made clear they needed to be isolated. This did not happen in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which was a significant oversight

a lack of financial support for care workers at the start of the pandemic made it difficult to allow them to stay away from their job if they were infected

long-standing weakness in the care sector, including financial struggles and staff shortages, exacerbated problems

by September 2020, evidence suggested care home visitors posed only a marginal infection risk, yet many care homes failed to ease restrictions in line with updated UK guidance, contributing to a significant decline in residents' health and wellbeing.

there was evidence of blanket do-not-resuscitate orders being put in place in some care homes, which is considered unlawful

millions of unpaid carers were left to take on evermore complex care and struggled because of a lack of support

Jean Adamson, of the Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, said: "Today's report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country's history.

"It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late."

Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating".

"When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed."

She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was.

"If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether."

Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues".

"That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added.

Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic.

She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives".

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course".

Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long.

"My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added.

articles.title: ‘Not getting involved’: US Vice President refuses to endorse Netanyahu
articles.summary: JD Vance’s comments follow Donald Trump’s backing of Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 elections.
articles.body:
United States Vice President JD Vance has declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of elections this month, saying he would prefer to stay on the sidelines and focus on midterm polls in the US.

Vance’s comments during an interview on Monday with journalist Mark Halperin came just a day after US President Donald Trump explicitly endorsed Netanyahu.

“I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him. I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

“I endorse American candidates and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” he added.

Vance last threw his weight behind a foreign leader in April, when he backed Hungary’s former right-wing Prime Minister Victor Orban, who lost in a landslide to Peter Magyar.

Over his two terms, Trump has cultivated a close relationship with Netanyahu and his right-wing government.

In his first term, Trump moved the US embassy to west Jerusalem, recognised Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights, withdrew from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and spearheaded a series of normalisation agreements with Arab countries that sidelined the Israel-Palestine issue.

Since taking office again in January 2025, the Trump administration has continued to sell weapons to Israel despite its genocidal war on Gaza, entered a conflict with Iran and escalated a crackdown on the International Criminal Court (ICC).

For his part, Vance, considered a likely 2028 presidential contender, has become emblematic of growing discontent within the Republican party over Washington’s unconditional support for Israel. That sentiment has deepened with the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has raised costs for US consumers.

While the vice president has said US support for Israel should continue, he has faced scepticism from Jewish Republicans about his commitment to the alliance.

In June, amid Israeli opposition to an Iran ceasefire plan, Vance told Israel: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have”.

He also warned Netanyahu’s cabinet against alienating Trump, calling the president “the only powerful ally” Israel has left.

It remains unclear whether Trump’s endorsement will boost Netanyahu’s Likud party ahead of the vote, with some opinion polls indicating wariness of the US president over his perceived attempts to restrain Israeli operations in Lebanon and resistance to further escalation in Iran.

Polls have shown the Yashar party leading Likud ahead of the October 27 vote. Its leader, former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, has said he will seek to build an opposition bloc to form a government.

articles.title: Drone attack kills over 150 people in South Sudan market, official says
articles.summary: South Sudanese officials said Sudan’s military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing over 150 people, one of the deadliest attacks in a war that has spilled across Sudan’s borders.
articles.body: NAIROBI, Kenya — South Sudanese officials said Sudan’s military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing over 150 people, one of the deadliest attacks in a war that has spilled across Sudan’s borders. The strike showed the lethality of airstrikes in Sudan’s war, which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), triggering a major humanitarian crisis and drawing in local militias and foreign powers. According to local authorities, the attack that hit the market in Abyei took place around midday on Monday. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information in Abyei, told Reuters on Tuesday that the death toll had jumped to 153 from 73. He said Sudan’s army was responsible for the attack, without providing evidence. A spokesperson for Sudan’s armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and an expert on the conflict told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market. The diplomatic sources said the depot had been used in the past by the RSF to supply its forces. A spokesperson for the RSF did not immediately respond to requests for comment. South Sudan declared independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have staked a claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. It borders Sudan’s Kordofan region, which has become a major center of fighting in Sudan’s war. Officials in Sudan’s military-led government told Reuters the RSF is active in parts of Abyei. Ngor denied the presence of the RSF in Abyei. Reuters could not immediately verify the claims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) warned in May that the presence of the RSF in Abyei had increased insecurity there, adding that delays in determining the disputed region’s final status had put civilians and UNISFA personnel at risk. Struggle to retrieve bodies Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. “It has reached 153 — those we can confirm killed and the number will even rise (further),” he said. “The fire is still burning. So the recovery process of the dead ones is still continuing. The situation is terrible.” Some 8,000 people had been displaced by Monday’s bombing, Ngor added. South Sudan’s foreign ministry said in a statement late on Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties. The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador in protest. Sudanese armed forces and the RSF have recently escalated drone strikes, with a series of attacks targeting RSF-held Nyala and army-held Khartoum airport this week. Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers said dozens of people were killed in attacks on October 17 and 18 in al-Muglad in West Kordofan state, attributing them to the Sudanese army. Chadian authorities have accused Sudan’s military of carrying out drone strikes on its territory, which UN experts say is regularly used by RSF supply lines. Sudan’s foreign ministry said in late August that its armed forces were acting to protect the country’s security. On October 10, an airstrike close to Sudan’s border with Egypt killed more than 70 artisanal miners, according to a local rights group. Patients treated for burns Abyei experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias. The attack is the deadliest in years to hit the area, where medical supplies and healthcare are scarce. South Sudan’s government says it has not taken sides in its neighbor’s war. However, diplomats and experts say Abyei has established itself as crucial, serving as a transit point for RSF logistics, particularly fuel. Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement posted late on Monday that it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital. “We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care,” said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at Ameth Bek Hospital. Photographs shared on MSF’s official social media account showed bandaged patients lying on the floor as they received care for their injuries.

articles.title: Artist who painted Jesus at age 8 tells Hannity she vanished for hours, experienced heaven
articles.summary: Akiane Kramarik, the child prodigy who painted "Prince of Peace" at age 8, told Sean Hannity about a childhood disappearance that baffled family.
articles.body: An apparent childhood disappearance sent Akiane Kramarik's family and police scrambling to find her, but the artist who famously painted Jesus at age 8 says she was somewhere no one thought to look. "I recall I am in this entire zone, I'm seeing my whole family and all the dogs and all of the police below," Kramarik said on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "It's as if I have like an eagle-eyes perspective." RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA Kramarik, 32, recalled feeling as though her body had "zoomed out" before everything went black. According to Kramarik, her disappearance sparked fears of a possible kidnapping, prompting family members, neighbors and police to launch a search. "My mom comes and she can't find me. My brothers search around the house, they couldn't find me. [They] call[ed] my dad. Every single neighbor, every friend... The police come, their dogs come, everybody is around the whole neighborhood searching for me. I'm missing, and no one knows where," she said. 'BLIND SIDE' STAR QUINTON AARON SAYS HE 'SAW JESUS' WHILE IN A COMA AFTER NEAR-FATAL STROKE "They think it was a potential kidnapping," she continued. "So my photo was displayed in all the town." Kramarik said she was just 5 years old when the incident occurred in Missouri, recalling that what she described as a journey through another realm corresponded to nearly seven hours of elapsed time, according to her parents. "My parents told me it was about six and a half, seven hours, something like that," she shared. During that time, Kramarik said God showed her extraordinary sights and imparted knowledge to her. She described the experience as lasting longer than the nearly seven hours she said she was missing. LOST CITY WHERE JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES HAS FINALLY BEEN IDENTIFIED, EXPERT SAYS Kramarik's account is one of several spiritual experiences she has described from her childhood, a period also marked by her exceptional artistic talent. At age 8, she painted "Prince of Peace," her now-famous portrait of Jesus that helped propel her to international recognition as a child prodigy. Kramarik said her otherworldly experience left a lasting impression that extended beyond her artwork. She said the experience also prompted her parents, who had raised their children in a nonreligious household, to reconsider their beliefs. articles.title: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark
articles.summary: Janine Lochrenberg, 65, was out on her daily morning swim with her club when she was attacked, her family tell the BBC.
articles.body:
A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.

Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.

Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.

Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.

She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.

Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.

She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".

"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.

Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.

"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."

Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.

Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

articles.title: Lavrov backs Tehran, but does Russia also gain from the US-Iran crisis?
articles.summary: Moscow pledges support to its sanctioned ally, but analysts say the war Iran wants to end has filled Russia’s coffers.
articles.body:
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov pledged Moscow’s support for Iran when he met his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday.

On Tuesday, Araghchi wrote on X: “Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now.”

But Russia’s position is not straightforward.

The war on Iran, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, has pushed up oil prices and handed Moscow a windfall. Washington has now also eased sanctions on Russian energy to bring down fuel costs – a major complaint from consumers in the US, who will shortly vote in mid-term elections.

So how close are Moscow and Tehran, and does Russia really want the US-Iran crisis to end? Here’s what you need to know:

To shore up a wartime partnership, and to shape what happens next.

Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera that with both countries fighting wars, Lavrov’s “primary motive is to solidify that alliance”.

He said the aim is to advance each side’s war goals: “Russia against Ukraine, Iran against the United States.”

But Hashemi said the main reason is that the US-Israeli attack has left the Middle East regional order unravelling, and Moscow wants a say in what replaces it.

“I suspect there’s a longer-term agenda here,” he said.

They have a strategic partnership, though their treaty stops short of a military alliance.

Putin and Pezeshkian signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Moscow in January 2025.

It came into force that October, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it has no mutual defence clause.

Ties deepened after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with Iran sharing Shahed drone technology that enabled Russia to build its own version.

In 2024, Washington accused Tehran of also sending Russia ballistic missiles.

In Tehran, Lavrov said Russian specialists who had left Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant – heavily damaged in US strikes – would gradually return.

Other countries are aware of the closeness of their relationship.

On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain for a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), and he was urged by its members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic Gulf waterway that Iran effectively closed shortly after the war began earlier this year.

Has Russia helped Iran in the war against the US?

The Russian Foreign Ministry has condemned what it called the “unlawful aggression” of the US and Israel, but Moscow has not intervened militarily.

US media outlets, citing intelligence reports, have said Russia and China supplied Iran with satellite imagery and weapons components. US President Donald Trump has dismissed those reports.

How has Russia benefitted from the US-Iran war?

After Iran effectively closed Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies are shipped during peacetime, the price of Brent crude rose from around $72 a barrel to as high as $120 a barrel in March and April. On Tuesday, Brent – the global benchmark – was trading at above $109 a barrel.

By April, revenue from Russia’s biggest oil tax had roughly doubled to about $9bn, according to Reuters calculations, as buyers unable to get supplies from the Gulf switched.

Since March, the US Treasury has issued waivers allowing sales of Russian oil already loaded at sea. This month, it waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027.

On Friday, Trump suspended newly passed sanctions on Russia and on buyers of its oil and gas. The move has sparked outrage among members of his own Republican Party who backed the sanctions bill.

On Sunday, he claimed he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table” in Ukraine talks.

“The Kremlin is using this opportunity to align Russian and American interests on Ukraine to try to stop Ukraine from continuing its attacks on Russian refineries,” John Lough, an associate fellow of the Russia and Eurasia Programme at Chatham House and a senior research fellow at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, told Al Jazeera.

“This has led to the breakdown of relations between Trump and Zelenskyy, which suits Moscow’s purposes because it is putting US policy in conflict with Europe’s policy on Ukraine,” he said.

So, does Russia really want the US-Iran war to end?

For now, Russia would appear to have every reason to want the stand-off between Washington and Tehran to continue, as it is “benefiting from higher oil prices and from the diesel squeeze that has encouraged Trump to lift sanctions and allow Russia to supply diesel to the US market,” Lough said.

But Nikita Smagin, an analyst on Russia’s role in the Middle East, told Al Jazeera on Monday that while Russia certainly has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, on balance, it likely does not want to see it escalate, as the consequences could be unpredictable.

Could Russia be an effective mediator in the US-Iran war?

Moscow talks to all sides caught up in this conflict, which Hashemi said gives it an edge over Washington. Much of the region has been affected as Iran has launched strikes against US military assets and energy infrastructure in the countries hosting US assets. These include Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.

Hashemi said Russia is “perfectly situated to shape a future new Middle East regional order” as “a major power that has direct diplomatic relations with all of the parties” in the region.

“The United States can’t make that claim because the United States has no relationship with Iran,” he said.

Putin has already acted as a channel with Washington, stating he relayed Iran’s views on ending the conflict to Trump in a phone call on October 9.

But Hashemi said he did not think “Trump is looking to Putin to help solve the Iran war”.

Trump’s Iran policy is shaped, he said, “first and foremost by Trump’s personal idiosyncrasies”, and then by his relationship with Israel, reflected among close advisers including Jared Kushner, Steve Witkoff and Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations.

Still, with Trump “in a quagmire”, Hashemi added: “I suspect that there are intense discussions between Russia and the United States.”

That could come to a head at a possible three-way summit.

Last month, the Kremlin said Putin and Trump had discussed meeting China’s President Xi Jinping to talk about the Ukraine war, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen in November, but the White House has not confirmed whether Trump will attend.

If such a meeting on Ukraine goes ahead, Hashemi said he suspects “the Iran war will also be part of the discussion”, with Trump looking to China and Russia “to see whether there’s any room there to help him negotiate an end to the war”.

On Monday, Lavrov said Moscow expects Pezeshkian to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow at the end of October.

Meanwhile, US and Iranian forces continue to fight for control of Hormuz ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

Trump has threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, but Araghchi responded by saying, “We have unfinished jobs, too.”
